title: The Pullman residence, Chicago
camera_position: from the southwest corner of Prairie Avenue and 18th Street, looking across the intersection; 18th Street recedes to the right toward the Fort Dearborn Massacre monument
creator: Detroit Publishing Co.
repository: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division
rights_basis: LoC: No known restrictions on publication
notes: Glass negative ('286' on negative; holder note 'Prarie Avenue'). Date bracket from Detroit Catalogue J (1901); the Fort Dearborn Massacre monument (erected 1893) is visible at the far right end of 18th Street, so the view is 1893 or later. The best in-period full view of the Pullman house's west (Prairie) and south (18th St) fronts: three-storey ashlar Second Empire block with mansard, iron roof cresting, pedimented dormers, ivy-covered walls, columned entrance porch on Prairie, corner/side porch on 18th, low stone-capped wall with piers along both sidewalks, lamp posts, young elms on parkway, unpaved/macadam roadway with stone crosswalk slabs and a carriage at the 18th St kerb. At the left edge, the neighbouring house to the north (1721 Prairie, Wirt Dexter house, identification by position) shows a broad columned front porch, gabled dormers and tall chimneys — useful for the Dexter house's 1889 Arthur Little front. Leafless trees: autumn/spring.

title: Pullman Residence, Chicago, The
camera_position: on 18th Street west of Calumet Avenue, beside the Fort Dearborn Massacre monument (right foreground), looking west-northwest along the south (18th Street) side of the Pullman property
creator: Detroit Publishing Co.
repository: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division
rights_basis: LoC: No known restrictions on publication
notes: Glass negative ('287' on negative; copyright 1900 blind stamp; holder notes 'Prairie Avenue' and 'Caption on monument: The Fort Dearborn Massacre'). Shows the 18th Street (south) flank of the Pullman house: the main mansarded block with its arched carriage/side entrance and stone balustraded porch, the long lower east wing with hipped roof and ivy (the later Beman additions/conservatory side), low stone wall with piers and shrubbery along 18th St, granite kerbs curving into Calumet Ave, gas/electric lamp standard, elm parkway trees and the monument's granite pedestal at right. Companion negative to LC-D4-12551 (same visit). Essential for the 18th St elevation and the extent of the east wing toward Calumet in c.1900.

title: South side of the Grosvenor house as built, c. 1870
creator: unknown photographer
repository: reproduced by Glessner House Museum (blog 'The Story of a House'); original holder not named
collection: The Early History of Prairie Avenue – Part IV (2020-07-07)
rights_basis: Blog reproduction with no rights statement; underlying c.1870 photograph likely public domain by age but holder/reproduction terms not established
notes: Narrow halftone crop (460x900 px) of a larger photograph. Blog says it is the only known photo showing the 1862 Cornelia Grosvenor house as originally built: two-storey brick Italianate, flat brick side wall with heavy bracketed eave cornice, panelled chimney, tall windows with hood mouldings, an ornate stone bay/porch with columns and balustrade at the front corner, and a low cast-iron balustrade fence on a stone curb. Pre-dates Jesse Spalding's severe remodelling, so it is NOT the 1904 appearance (see the remodelled view). Useful for the original masonry shell that survived inside the remodel.

title: Wirt Dexter house prior to front addition, c. 1888 (Photo by George Glessner)
camera_position: from the west side of Prairie Avenue opposite 1721, in winter
creator: George Glessner
repository: Glessner House Museum (George Glessner photographs; per blog caption)
collection: The Early History of Prairie Avenue – Part IV (2020-07-07)
rights_basis: Museum photograph reproduced on blog; no rights statement
notes: Winter view by George Glessner (the Glessners' son, an amateur photographer) of the 1863 frame Dexter house BEFORE Arthur Little's 1889 brick front addition: two-storey clapboard house with central front gable (round attic window), shuttered windows, bracketed eaves, a square cupola/belvedere and several tall chimneys, ground-floor bays, a low stone wall along the sidewalk with gate piers, a gas street lamp in the foreground; the neighbouring house at right (south, toward Pullman) shows brick bays. Because the 1889 addition was built nearly to the lot line, the 1904 frontage looked very different; this documents the original block that stood behind the addition until a later owner demolished it.

camera_position: from the Prairie Avenue sidewalk in front of the house
creator: unknown photographer
repository: reproduced by Glessner House Museum (blog); original holder not named

rights_basis: Blog reproduction; no rights statement
notes: The 1853 John N. Staples house (first house on Prairie Ave): stuccoed/painted two-storey Italianate with low hipped roof, deep bracketed cornice, square glazed cupola/observatory, a two-storey wrap-around porch (turned columns, open balustraded upper deck), tall windows, a canted bay at right, lattice-skirted porch base and an ornate picket fence with turned balusters. Roberts Gothic Revival ('Hudson River Gothic') house: steep front gable with crocketed finial and oculus, paired pointed-arch windows with hood moulds, a canted ground-floor bay with pointed lights, a polygonal corner tower with pointed windows and a tall conical/pyramidal slate roof, a Gothic entrance porch with pierced brackets over a stoop, a lower wing at left, and gate piers with an iron fence. title: Left: 1706 S. Prairie Avenue / Right: 1700 S. Prairie Avenue.
addresses: 1638 S. Prairie Avenue (neighbour, at right edge)
1708 S. Prairie Avenue (neighbour, at left edge)
camera_position: from the east side of Prairie Avenue, nearly square to the pair
creator: unknown photographer
repository: Chicagology (secondary reproduction; original holder not named — possibly Glessner House Museum)
rights_basis: Secondary web reproduction; source not stated
notes: The Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge Georgian Revival double townhouse built 1901–02 for the Glessner children: a continuous three-storey dark-brick block under a slate mansard with pedimented dormers and a wooden roof balustrade (Chinese-Chippendale pattern); stone keystoned flat-arched windows on the second floor, round-arched first-floor windows with iron balconettes; two mirror-image columned entrance porticoes with balconies above, at the outer ends; iron area railings. At the right edge the steep-gabled Gothic Revival house with pointed windows = 1638 (Gregory), immediately north — the 1600 and 1700 blocks were continuous (no through 17th Street; see the atlas crop record). At left a rusticated stone-trimmed three-storey neighbour = 1708 (James Ward Thorne residence by 1911; cf. the 'Christmas tree' photograph, which captions the same three houses as 1708, 1706, 1700). Caption labels left = 1706, right = 1700 (north unit), consistent with a view from the east. The same photograph appears (sepia, sharper) on the Glessner House blog post 'Kodak plant demolition begins' (2015-03-10) captioned 'Glessner townhouses, 1700-1706 S. Prairie Avenue, Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge, architects'. Strong evidence for the 1904 appearance; townhouses demolished 1954 for the Kodak plant expansion.
